summary:
NASA has spent decades studying how fire behaves in microgravity, but finding a specific result can mean digging through reports and experiment tables. We built Flame in Freefall to make that research easier to use.

Researchers, students and engineers can ask questions in English or Spanish about 24 combustion investigations in NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository. The assistant searches the documents and provides answers with citations, including page numbers when available. When it can’t find enough evidence, it says so.

A dashboard beside the chat displays charts, tables and rankings from the experiment data, letting users check the numbers behind an answer.

The system combines search across 39 reports and science documents with a knowledge graph connecting investigations, hardware, materials and experimental conditions. Our goal is to help people find and understand research that could inform fire safety in spacecraft and future lunar habitats.
details:
We started with a practical problem: NASA’s combustion research contains valuable findings, but those findings are spread across documents and tables from many different investigations. Finding an answer takes time, especially when you need to trace it back to the original experiment.

Flame in Freefall brings those sources into one place. Users ask questions in a chat, and the assistant searches the PSI documents for relevant evidence. Answers arrive as streaming text and include citations so users can check the sources themselves. Any additional explanation drawn from general model knowledge is labeled separately.

For questions involving numbers, the app reads the experiment tables and displays the results on a dashboard beside the conversation. Users can request tables, scatter plots and rankings through the chat. The plotted values come from the stored experiment data.

The app supports English and Spanish, saved conversations, user accounts and a choice of three answer models.
